t: Plan and aim of the session
n: In this session we will talk about forensic chemical examination, forensic chemists, their duties, ethics and deontology. This is laboratory session 2. The plan has two points: the first is forensic chemical examination, the second is forensic chemists, their duties, ethics and deontology. Forensic chemical examination has mainly two aims. The first is to assist judicial and investigative staff. The second is to assist health care workers in preventing poisoning.

Now let us consider what the examination determines. The examination determines whether toxic substances that harm human health or lead to death are present, and their quality and quantity. It also helps medical workers to improve medical care for the population and to prevent poisoning. In order to give rapid medical care to a poisoned person, the examination may be carried out on the instruction of the judicial and investigative authorities or on a written instruction from the hospital.

Analysis is divided into directed and non-directed. Directed analysis is carried out on the instruction of judicial and investigative staff for one or several substances. In non-directed, that is general, analysis the specimen is tested for the 67 toxic and potent substances listed in the decision. If no substance is named in the decision, the specimen is tested for the toxic substances approved by the ministry. This is also seen in the table: in directed analysis the substances named in the instruction are tested, while in non-directed analysis the 67 substances of the decision are tested.

In forensic chemistry laboratories, depending on how the task is set, analysis is divided into complete and incomplete. In incomplete analysis the expert chemist, on a separate instruction, tests for one or several toxic substances; this corresponds to directed analysis. In complete analysis the expert is obliged to test for all the toxic substances on the list in the ministry's decision. This includes volatile and metallic poisons, as well as the acidified water and alcohol group and the solvent group.

t: Groups of poisons in complete analysis
n: Let us give examples of groups of poisons in complete analysis. The group of volatile poisons includes hydrocyanic acid, alcohols, formaldehyde, chloroform, chloral hydrate, carbon tetrachloride, dichloroethane, phenol and cresols. Metal-containing poisons include salts of barium, manganese, chromium, zinc, thallium, lead, copper, mercury, bismuth, cadmium, silver, arsenic and antimony. Barbiturates, alkaloids and synthetic substances are isolated by the acidified water and alcohol method. Pesticides are isolated with an organic solvent.

Let us move on to the legal basis. The organisation of forensic medical examination is based on the Law "On Forensic Examination", which came into force on 1 June 2010. The Law was approved by the Legislative Chamber on 18 November 2009 and by the Senate on 7 May 2010. According to Presidential Resolution No. PP-4049 of 4 December 2018, the Main Bureau was transformed into the Republican Scientific and Practical Centre of Forensic Medical Examination. The bureaus of the regions and of the city of Tashkent were reorganised as branches of the Centre.

Let us review the chronology of regulatory documents. Initially, the organisation of forensic medical examination was based on the code of judicial procedure and the resolution of the People's Commissariat of 4 July 1939. Then the guide to organisation was issued on 13 December 1952, and in 1957 the rules for the examination of physical evidence. The present basis is the Law "On Forensic Examination", in force since 1 June 2010, and the 2018 Resolution No. PP-4049. The table gives these years in order: 1939, 1952, 1957, 2010 and 2018.

Now let us see who directs the examination. Forensic medical and forensic chemical examination is directed by the Chief Forensic Medical Expert at the ministry. In managerial matters he is subordinate to the Ministry of Health or its first deputy. In scientific and practical work he is subordinate to the research institute of forensic medicine. That is, one post has a double subordination: in management to the ministry, in scientific and practical work to the institute.

The Republican Centre consists of several departments. The organisational and methodological department works together with the quality control department, and there is also a department of complex examinations. The medico-criminalistic department has a spectral and radiological unit. In the forensic biology department there operates a unit for molecular genetic examination of DNA. The forensic chemistry department is organised together with a biochemical investigation unit. Another department is forensic histology. For us the main one is the forensic chemistry department.

t: Rooms of the forensic chemistry department
n: Let us consider the rooms of the forensic chemistry department. The department must have at least 5 rooms; the number and purposes of the rooms are specified in the Rules approved by the Chief Forensic Medical Expert. The first room is for receiving and storing objects, and a special refrigerator and an iron safe are allocated to it. The second is the investigation laboratory; the third are rooms for sample preparation and study of the external appearance. The fourth are working rooms, that is offices. The fifth is a room for storing reagents and other materials.

The laboratory regime is strict. All rooms of the laboratory are locked and sealed after work. A separately built cold room for storing physical evidence and separate rooms for storing poisonous substances are mandatory. The posts are also defined: the forensic chemistry department has a senior chemist, who is considered the head, and the posts of chemist and laboratory assistant. Remember: separate storage places are required for objects and for poisons.

Let us list the duties of the forensic chemist. First, to carry out forensic chemical examination on the basis of decisions of judicial and investigative authorities and, in some cases, at the request of forensic medical experts and medical institutions. Second, on being summoned by judicial and investigative authorities, to attend to answer questions under any conditions. Third, on completion of the examination, to set out the result of the analysis, that is a report is drawn up. There are also requirements: to hold higher education in pharmacy, to complete a specialisation course and to complete a refresher course every 5 years.

Now let us dwell on the rights of the expert chemist. He may familiarise himself with the case materials and demand additional materials. He is also entitled to be present at the judicial and investigative sessions held in the case. The rights of experts are equated with the rights of forensic medical experts. The table gives duties and rights side by side. In the duties column: carrying out examination on a decision, attending when summoned, writing the report, higher education and a course every 5 years. In the rights column: familiarisation with materials, demanding additional materials and attending sessions.

t: Duties of the expert (text of the Law)
n: The duties of the expert are set out in the text of the Law. The expert examines the submitted objects comprehensively and fully and gives a reasoned and objective conclusion on the questions. He attends in person when summoned by the inquiry, investigation or court, and answers additional questions to explain his conclusion. He does not disclose information that has become known to him in connection with the examination; he ensures the safekeeping of objects and case materials. He has no right to communicate the result to anyone other than the body, that is the person, who ordered the examination, nor to collect materials independently.

The word deontology comes from the Greek deon, meaning that which is necessary, and logos, meaning teaching. It is knowledge that studies the aims and regularities of fully clarifying a case. The ethics and deontology of the forensic chemist are equally and directly linked to the norms of law. In conversation with the victim or relatives, the expert does not raise his voice and does not ask questions that hurt self-esteem or that are inappropriate. Honesty, truthfulness and fairness are required of the expert. Keeping the causes of the incident confidential is his professional duty.

Let us look at the main directions of ethics and deontology. The activity of a medical worker is based on a high standard of ethics and deontological rules; these requirements do not change even after the patient's death. The worker is obliged to carry out diagnosis and treatment conscientiously regardless of the patient's sex, age, religion, nationality and social status. He provides quality, effective and safe medical care; if resources are lacking, he refers the patient to a suitable institution. The diagram shows the directions: attitude to the patient, confidentiality, truthfulness, professional knowledge, information and safety.

Now about confidentiality and liability. According to the Fundamentals of Health Protection Legislation, experts who disclose examination data are held administratively liable for breach of professional duty. The fact that a citizen sought medical help, the state of his health and his diagnosis constitute medical confidentiality. Disclosure of this secret without the consent of the citizen or his legal representative is not permitted. The cases listed in the book are an exception.

There are cases in which the secret may be disclosed without consent. The first: for the purpose of examining and treating a citizen who, because of the severity of his condition, cannot express his wishes. The second: when there is a threat of the spread of infectious diseases, mass poisoning and injury. The third: in connection with an investigation or court proceedings, at the request of the bodies of inquiry and investigation, the prosecutor's office and the court. The fourth: when help is given to a person under eighteen, to inform the parents, and also when harm is suspected to have been caused by unlawful acts.

t: Observing the law even under pressure
n: An important rule of ethics: observing the law even under pressure. A medical worker, in any conditions, including when pressure is exerted by natural and legal persons, is obliged to refuse to act contrary to the law and moral rules. Aggressive influence on the physical and psychological state of patients under examination or suspected of involvement in a crime is forbidden. If torture, violence or treatment demeaning to human dignity is noticed, this is reported to the head and to the relevant state bodies.

Truthfulness and non-tolerance of corruption are also part of ethics. A medical worker is strictly forbidden to give an incorrect or inaccurate conclusion, as well as all kinds of fraud. Medical workers are also forbidden to make unlawful agreements among themselves, with pharmacists and with other persons, and to enter into corrupt relations. In completing case histories, reports and medical and other documents, one must be impartial and truthful.

t: Professional knowledge and compliance with documents
n: On professional knowledge and compliance with documents. Every medical worker must constantly improve his knowledge and skills and regularly take part in events that contribute to professional development. The worker must become familiar with all codes, laws and subordinate legislation relating to his professional activity and comply with them. He must also be aware of all existing standards, protocols and clinical recommendations. For his actions and advice in the mass media and on the internet the worker is fully answerable to citizens and to the medical community.

Let us also recall other ethical requirements. A medical worker has no right to interfere without grounds in the personal and family life of patients. In the wide application of modern methods, every worker must ensure the highest level of safety for patients. When side effects and complications of medicines are identified, they are reported to the head and to the authorised state bodies. The worker must refrain from actions that weaken respect for his profession and tarnish his honour.

Let us look at the obligations and prohibitions in ethics side by side. Obligations: despite pressure, the worker refuses to act contrary to the law and moral rules, provides quality and safe medical care, constantly improves his qualifications, completes documents truthfully, and reports side effects. Prohibited: an incorrect and inaccurate conclusion, fraud and corrupt agreements, aggression against suspects, covert treatment methods, and unjustified interference in private life. Covert methods and means of treatment must not be used with regard to the life and health of citizens.

t: What the investigation plan is based on
n: Let us see what the investigation plan is based on. Physical evidence is often an irreplaceable object, so the expert draws up a clear plan and works carefully and economically. The bases of the plan are shown in the diagram: the referral from the judicial authorities and full study of the causes of death, the case history, the report of the forensic medical examination, the pH, odour and colour of the specimen and the presence of foreign substances, and the results of the preliminary tentative examination. The preliminary examination helps to exclude many toxic substances or to suggest which poison may be present. If the tentative examination is positive, the main examination for the suspected poison is mandatory.

The preliminary examination has possibilities and limitations. There are very many substances that cause poisoning, so testing every specimen for every poison would take a great deal of time. The preliminary examination is carried out mainly in blood, urine, lavage fluid or a small quantity of the specimen with sensitive reactions. It helps to exclude many poisons, to suggest a possible poison, and saves time and specimen. But some tentative methods, although highly sensitive, are not specific. No conclusion can be drawn on this basis.

t: Decision on examination and accompanying documents
n: On the decision on examination and the accompanying documents. The decision ordering the examination must state the commission of the crime, the physical evidence and the questions put to the forensic chemist. A written record of the decision, an extract from the forensic medical report and, if the patient was in hospital, an extract from the case history are sent to the laboratory. If the decision does not state which toxic substances to test for, the specimen is tested for the toxic substances approved by the ministry.

Practical exercise: receiving physical evidence. The record of the decision, an extract from the forensic medical report and from the case history are sent. The physical evidence and the documents sent with it are entered in the laboratory's registration log, then handed to the expert. If the packaging of the physical evidence is damaged, the examination is carried out after a report is drawn up. The procedure in the diagram is the same: decision and accompanying documents, entry in the log, handing to the expert, and a report if the packaging is damaged.

On the documents of the examination. In forensic chemical examination laboratories mainly 3 logs are kept. The first is the registration log, consisting of 16 sections. The second is the forensic chemist's working notebook, in which all calculations relating to the day-to-day examination are recorded. The third is the book of reports: the handwritten book of forensic chemical examination reports, like the working notebook, is numbered, bound with cord and sealed.

The final stage of the investigation is writing the investigation report or the expert's conclusion. The report is drawn up on the basis of the entries in the working notebook after thorough study of the results. The report consists of 4 parts. The first is the introduction, the second is the description of the appearance, the third is the chemical investigation, and the fourth is the expert's conclusion. Remember the sequence of these parts.

t: Introduction and appearance in the report
n: Let us consider the first parts of the report. The introduction states on the basis of which document and in which laboratory the investigation was made, the expert's full name, post, degree and working notebook. Also recorded are the victim's full name, the evidence sent, the time the investigation began and ended, and the toxic substances to be tested for. The appearance section records the full appearance of the physical evidence, packaging, container, sealing, inscriptions on the packaging, colour, odour, weight and pH of the medium.

t: Chemical investigation and conclusion in the report
n: The chemical investigation is considered the main part of the report. In it, the methods, reactions, reagents and devices, and quantitative calculations are recorded in order on the basis of the working notebook. In this part of the report it is forbidden to write various chemical formulae or to cite the name of any author. In the conclusion, the toxic substances found are stated first; the quantity is calculated in mg per 100 g of physical evidence. Then the toxic substances for which a complete chemical investigation was made and a negative result obtained are stated.

Rules for completing and storing the report. When ethyl alcohol is detected in blood and urine, the report is printed in two copies, sealed by the expert chemist, and the time of writing is stated. The seal of the forensic medical examination is applied to the report; one copy is sent to the relevant organisation and the other is kept in the archive of the forensic medical examination. A preserved specimen is kept for up to 1 year; documents are kept in a safe and are destroyed after 1 year. Specimens containing alcohol are destroyed after 1 month.

t: The examination process: from receipt to archive
n: Let us review the examination process from receipt to archive. Physical evidence is sent to the forensic chemistry laboratory through the office, that is the chancellery, and is entered in the registration log together with its documents. The expert chemist is responsible for keeping the physical evidence from the start of the examination to its end; work is carried out according to the plan he has drawn up. After the investigation a report is drawn up and sealed. When ethyl alcohol is detected in blood and urine, the report is printed in two copies: one is sent to the organisation and the other is kept in the archive.

Now the history of acute poisoning centres. The second part of toxicological chemistry is express analysis of specimens in centres for the treatment of acute poisoning. The increase in cases of acute poisoning after 1950-1960 set new tasks for the health service. The table shows that in 1961 a toxicological team was opened in Moscow, and in 1963 a centre at the Sklifosovsky Institute. In 1964 a children's centre was opened at the Filatov Hospital, and in 1966 centres in Leningrad and Alma-Ata. By the order of the Ministry of Health of 6 May 1980, determination and treatment departments began work in all centres. In 1987 narcological laboratories were opened.

t: Circumstances taken into account in assessing the result
n: Certain circumstances are taken into account in assessing the result, especially when no poison is found. The substance may have been eliminated from the body before death or may have undergone metabolic change. The substance may have decomposed completely or combined with other substances. A substance may also remain undetected because the sensitivity of the method is low. When a substance is detected, quantitative analysis is always carried out, because in some cases reactions characteristic of a harmless substance may occur.

t: A detected substance is not always a poison
n: A detected substance does not always mean a poison. If the reaction is positive, the following circumstances must be considered. The victim may have taken the substance as a medicine. The detected substance may be naturally present in the specimen, for example metals. As a result of putrefaction of the specimen, compounds giving a reaction characteristic of the substance under examination may have formed. Some substance may have been added to the specimen under examination from the external environment. If no poison is found, the substance may have been eliminated before death, may have undergone metabolism, or the sensitivity of the method may have been low.

Let us repeat the key numbers to remember. The forensic chemistry department has at least 5 rooms; the expert completes a refresher course every 5 years. 3 logs are kept in the laboratory; the registration log consists of 16 sections, and the report of 4 parts. A preserved specimen is kept for up to 1 year, a specimen containing alcohol for 1 month. These numbers are often asked in the test.

Let us conclude. The examination serves two aims: assistance to judicial investigation and the prevention of poisoning. As to documents, 3 logs and a 4-part report are kept. Retention periods: a preserved specimen up to 1 year, documents 1 year, an alcohol-containing specimen 1 month. The main rules of ethics: observing the law even under pressure, keeping confidentiality, a truthful conclusion and refusal of unlawful agreements.

Review questions. First: what forensic chemical examination is and what aims it serves; what directed and non-directed analysis are. Second: the rooms and posts of the forensic chemistry department; the duties and rights of the forensic chemist. Third: the parts of the forensic chemical investigation report, the logs, and the retention periods for physical evidence and documents. Fourth: the rules of ethics and deontology of the medical worker and medical confidentiality.
